# Why R?

::: {.r-fit-text}

> There are only two kinds of languages: the ones people complain about and the ones 
nobody uses.
> 
> -- Bjarne Stroustrup \(creator of the C++ programming language\)

:::


## What is R? 

::: columns
::: column



::: {.fragment fragment-index=1}

- An open-source clone of **S**, which was a programming language developed at the Bell Telephone Laboratories in 1976. 

:::
::: {.fragment fragment-index=3}

- A language built for working with data
:::
::: {.fragment fragment-index=4}

  - With all the features of a general purpose language
  - plus functional programming
  - and at least [5 object-oriented systems](https://www.reddit.com/r/rstats/comments/1sk313c/why_r_has_four_oop_systems_s3_s4_r5_r6/)

:::
:::
::: column

![](images/meme-pirate-favorite-letter.jpg){fig-alt="A skeleton army with text 'Rule 6 of the pirate code: What's a pirate's favorite letter?'" width="80%" fragment-index=2 .fragment}
:::
:::

## Pros and Cons

::: columns
::: column
Pros:

- Excellent packages for data graphics
- Interactive and responsive
- Tons of tutorials and materials
  - [Big book of R](https://www.bigbookofr.com) - TONS of free online textbooks
  - [Tidy Tuesday videos](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PL19ev-r1GBwkuyiwnxoHTRC8TTqP8OEi8) - how to clean, analyze, and visualize data in R
- Supportive community - [R ladies+](https://rladies.org/programs/), [{{< fa brands reddit title="Reddit logo">}}](https://reddit.com/r/rstats), [{{< fa brands bluesky title="Bluesky logo" >}} #rstats](https://bsky.app/hashtag/Rstats), [{{< fa brands bluesky title="Bluesky logo" >}} #statistics](https://bsky.app/hashtag/statistics)

:::
::: column
Cons

- Optimizes programmer time - computing time can be slower
  - Industry uses R for prototyping, Python/C for production
- Easy to write bad/hard-to-maintain code    
[This is true in almost every language]{.fragment .cerulean-dk .emph}
- Different conventions than C/Python/Java    
[Counting from 1, 2, 3, ... rather than 0, 1, 2, ...]{.fragment .cerulean-dk .emph}

:::
:::

# Why Not Spreadsheets?

1. Reproducibility. Code is like a recipe, Spreadsheets are one-off analyses. Things get changed accidentally.
2. Spreadsheet references are less readable than variable names
3. It's best to separate data, code, and output. Spreadsheets mix them.
4. Spreadsheet functionality is limited compared to add-on libraries
5. [Excel charts are terrible (personal opinion)]{.cerulean .emph .fragment}

# Importing Data into R

## Getting Started

1. Open RStudio
2. Open an Editor window (by default, a text file in the top left corner)

## Setting Up  

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| collapse: false
library(readr) # <1> 
library(dslabs) # <2>

path <- system.file("extdata", package="dslabs") # <3>

files <- list.files(path) # <4>
files
```
1. Read in files efficiently
2. Package to go with the IDS books
3. Find the folder with external data files (`extdata`) in the `dslabs` package
4. What files are in the `extdata` folder?


## Setting Up

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| collapse: false
files <- list.files(path, full.names = T) # <1>
files
```

1. List the files AND the path where the files are located
 


## Reading in a CSV file

::: callout-note
### CSV
Comma Separated Value. Different columns are separated by comma characters (`,`). Any field that contains a comma must be quoted.
:::

::: columns
::: {.column width="60%"}

```{r} 
#| echo: true

carbon_df <- read_csv(files[3])         # <1> 
names(carbon_df) <- c("Year", "TotalC") # <2>
head(carbon_df)                         # <3>

```
1. Read in the third file in the list, which ends in `carbon_emissions.csv`
2. Rename columns to have shorter names
3. Look at the head (the first 6 rows, by default) of the object


:::
::: {.column width="40%"}
::: callout
### File contents
```{r}
#| echo: false

readLines(files[3])[1:10]
```
:::
:::
:::


## More Complicated CSVs

```{r}
#| echo: true

problems(olive_df) # <1>
```
1. When a CSV is not properly formatted, problems can pile up. Use `problems()` to see what R is complaining about. 


## More Complicated CSVs

```{r}
#| echo: true

readLines(files[8])[1:10] # <1>
```
1. When in doubt, look at the first few lines of the file. Count how many columns in several rows manually. Then come up with a hypothesis and a plan.

## CSV Trick: Separate the Names from the Data

```{r}
#| echo: true
olive_df <- read_csv(files[8],  # <1> 
                     col_names = FALSE, # <2>
                     skip = 1) # <3>
olive_names <- read_csv(files[8], col_names = FALSE, n_max = 1) # <4>
olive_names <- as.character(olive_names) # <5>
olive_names <- c("row", "RegionName", olive_names[-1]) # <6>
names(olive_df) <- olive_names # <7>
head(olive_df)
```
1. Read in the same file, but with additional arguments
2. Tell `read_csv` you're not providing column names
3. Skip the first line of the file
4. Read in only the first line of the file
5. Convert the table to a vector (a list)
6. Add names for the first two columns (row, RegionName) and remove the empty entry (`olive_names[-1]`). Put everything into the same vector using `c(...)`
7. Set the names of the table

## RStudio Projects

- Help you keep track of the files for a data science project
- File -> New Project -> New Directory 
  - Name your new project something descriptive
  - Put the project in sensible folder

- Move data into the project folder (into a `data/` subdirectory if multiple files)
- .R files in the project folder will find your data automatically without needing a file path.
